seasons.review_body: Beyond Evil aired on JTBC from February 19 to April 10, 2021, sweeping the 57th Baeksang Arts Awards with Best Drama, Best Screenplay, and Best Actor for Shin Ha-kyun. The series places two officers, the demoted, eccentric Dong-sik and the elite Seoul transplant Joo-won, in a provincial town where a 20-year-old serial murder case reopens. Writer Kim Su-jin builds the thriller around mutual suspicion: each detective privately suspects the other is the killer. The structure stays ambiguously balanced and the show does not resolve its moral questions cleanly. IMDb audience scores settle at 8.1. The series draws inspiration from the Hwaseong murders case without fictionality turning exploitative. Shin Ha-kyun and Yeo Jin-goo sustain a two-lead tension that is rare in procedural drama.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Beyond Evil S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Lee Dong Sik** is singing when trouble moves toward him. A call says he needs to be fetched quickly. At the live café, a customer dispute escalates, and the song stops. The hour understands interruption as its cleanest weapon: music gives way to police work, police work gives way to arrest, and arrest gives way to a question about a dead sister. BollyAI's read: this pilot works best when procedure tightens around character, one legal step at a time. Its weakness comes from the same engine in excess. The middle can feel like code before pulse.

## The Song Stops Before the Case Begins

The first move is simple and useful. **Oh Ji Hun** calls that it is nothing, but Dong Sik needs to be fetched quickly. That contradiction matters because the episode keeps treating “nothing” as the lie people tell before a case becomes official. Dong Sik’s singing at the live café is not throwaway colour. It places him in a public room, performing ease, until the customer dispute pulls him back into duty.

That is a smart introduction because the episode does not hand Dong Sik a neat biography. It defines him through friction. He tries to avoid trouble while policing allegations, yet the world keeps manufacturing the kind of trouble that sticks to a cop. The stop-start rhythm suits him: a man caught between a community scene and a police file.

The cut from café energy to investigation also gives the hour its shape. This is a pilot about escalation, but not the loud action kind. A casual dispute becomes an allegation. An allegation becomes a room full of suspects. The room becomes a legal problem. The episode’s best instinct is to make bureaucracy feel like a trapdoor.

## Procedure Becomes a Trap

The Salon de Manyang incident is where the hour stops circling and starts filing charges. An assault or attempted assault case involving Dong Sik is reported, and soon everyone in the room is declared under arrest. That hard turn announces the show’s procedural appetite. The episode is not satisfied with the incident as drama. It wants the exact charge basis, the classification, the mechanism by which chaos becomes a case.

That gives the sequence bite. Dong Sik, introduced as someone trying to stay out of trouble, is suddenly tied to a mass arrest environment involving gambling and fraud implications. The point is not whether he controls the room. The room controls him. Once the law enters, proximity becomes dangerous.

The legal turn is strong, but it arrives with such density that character feeling briefly falls behind paperwork. The episode can be precise, then airless. It wants the audience inside the machinery of policing, and that ambition pays off later, but here the machinery clanks loudly enough to drown out some emotional shading.

Still, the escalation has purpose. It teaches the rules of the show’s world: procedure does not clean up disorder. It gives disorder a sharper knife.

## Han Ju Won Treats the Law Like a Locked Door

**Han Ju Won** enters the pilot as a man who wants procedure to hold. Around the missing-person discussion, he pushes the legal limits of what can be reported, especially around the category of a “child” missing report. The contradiction is clear. He wants proper process, yet uses process as a gate, denying or redirecting the missing report because the legal frame does not fit cleanly.

That makes him more interesting than a standard rule-following inspector. He is procedure under pressure. In his hands, the law becomes a lock he keeps testing from both sides. When the chief insists on missing-person reporting, the discussion turns into a fight over categories, and the pilot’s larger obsession sharpens: what happens when a human emergency arrives in the wrong legal shape?

The downside is pacing. The dossier’s rhythm points to long mid-episode stretches of dialogue-to-dialogue procedural density, with pauses that suggest authority landing, disputes cooling, or scene pressure resetting. That structure can create menace, but it can also flatten momentum. The pilot asks for patience here.

The patience is partly rewarded because Ju Won’s caution later curdles into direct interrogation. The man who resists misclassification begins acting as if an old case is actionable.

## A Missing Patient Keeps the World Human

The search for Mr. Bang, the missing dementia patient, gives the hour a needed human-scale counterweight. Dong Sik is not just orbiting allegations and legal debates. He is out looking for someone vulnerable, trying to locate a person who can slip through the cracks without any grand conspiracy required.

This beat matters because it shows the procedural system at its most ordinary. The instruction about not making reports on a personal phone from now on is small, and the smallness matters. Police work here is accusation, arrest, operational control, repeated mistakes, bad channels, and the effort to stop one messy report from becoming the next avoidable problem.

The Mr. Bang stretch also helps Dong Sik. He is most watchable when the episode lets him work rather than explain himself. After the Salon de Manyang turn, the search gives him a practical objective, a way to move through the story without the episode overstating his interior life. His contradictions stay active. He is a cop trying to manage trouble while trouble keeps attaching itself to his name.

Here, the pilot finds a better balance. The case mechanics remain, but they are tied to a body in the world, a person who needs finding, and an officer whose competence has immediate stakes.

## The Dinner Sings Off Key

The dinner scene with **Oh Ji Hwa** telling Ju Won to memorize and sing properly sounds, on paper, like a tonal detour. In practice, it fits the episode’s design. The pilot keeps putting official people into unofficial rooms, then watching the performance crack. At the café, Dong Sik’s song is interrupted by disorder. At dinner, Ju Won is pressured into a social script he has not mastered.

That contrast is useful. Dong Sik belongs to the room until the case drags him out. Ju Won does not belong, and the demand that he sing properly makes that visible without needing a speech. The scene turns social ease into another procedure: learn the words, hit the cue, do not expose the wrong thing.

It also gives the hour texture before the final hard pivot. Without this dinner, the pilot risks becoming a line of police conversations with different labels. With it, the episode shows that control is legal, cultural, social, and personal. Ju Won’s discomfort around a song rhymes with his discomfort around a report: he wants the correct form, but the room asks for something messier.

The scene is tense because nobody needs to draw a weapon. A wrong note is enough.

## The Sister Turns the Pilot Into an Accusation

The final movement is the pilot’s cleanest hook. Inspector Han orders that **Lee Yu Yeon** is the sister, then pushes the question of whether she was killed. The episode has spent its running time teaching the weight of categories: assault or attempted assault, gambling charges, missing-person limits, proper reporting channels. Then it lands on the category that cuts through all of them: sister.

That is the sharp move. Lee Yu Yeon is not introduced here as an abstract cold-case label. Her identity becomes the pressure point that turns investigation into accusation. The open questions work because they are specific: why Ju Won is interrogating this sister identity in relation to an unidentified body, what he suspects about a cold-case killer connection to Dong Sik, and how the earlier missing-report law will matter when the case widens.

The ending does more than add mystery. It reorders the hour behind it. Dong Sik’s attempts to avoid trouble, the arrest environment, the procedural arguments, and Ju Won’s legal rigidity all begin pointing toward the same darker center. The pilot waits until the end to name what it has been circling.

The route there is sometimes heavy. The landing is clean.

## The Verdict

“Episode 1” is a dense, confident pilot that turns local disorder into procedural pressure before revealing the colder case underneath. Its best craft choice is escalation through classification: every report, charge, and legal limit narrows the space around Dong Sik and Ju Won. The weaker stretch is the mid-episode density, where the legal talk can feel more explanatory than dramatic. Still, the hour earns its final question because it has built a world where paperwork and suspicion feed each other. Dong Sik emerges as a man trouble keeps finding, while Ju Won becomes dangerous precisely because he believes in correct procedure until he decides suspicion is stronger. As a season opener, it plants the cold-case spine clearly: Lee Yu Yeon’s identity is the wound the episode saves for last.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere drops Joo-won into Manyang and places him alongside the notorious Dong-sik, whose reputation as the local oddity the episode never overplays. The discovery of a skeleton in the first act signals what kind of thriller this will be: patient, provincial, menacing.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The first exchange between Dong-sik and Joo-won establishes the show's central unresolved question before either character has said anything that should raise it.

verdict.one_liner: A dense pilot turns local disorder into legal pressure, then lands its cold-case hook with a clean accusation.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 15
episode_reviews.review_body: Beyond Evil's penultimate episode arrives as the series' most dramatically pressurised hour - the accumulated weight of fourteen episodes of mutual suspicion collapsing into its most direct confrontation. Joo-won's moral framework, built on a faith in institutional law and a certainty about who he is, has been incrementally dismantled across the season by everything Dong-sik represents about what justice actually requires in a place the system has failed. Episode 15 is where the dismantling reaches completion. Kim Su-jin's script delivers the confrontation the thriller's structure has been promising without releasing the tension early - the episode ends not in resolution but in the kind of suspended moral ambiguity that makes the finale necessary rather than merely concluding. The two lead performances here match the material at the level of the series' Baeksang sweep.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Penultimate episode where the accumulated suspicion reaches its breaking point. The series' most dramatically pressurised hour, with Joo-won's moral framework finally failing under the weight of what Dong-sik represents.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Dong-sik speaks to Joo-won with a warmth that is either genuine or the show's most unsettling misdirection - the scene divides viewers to this day.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 16
episode_reviews.review_body: Beyond Evil's finale resolves its central question with the moral precision the series earned across sixteen episodes. Writer Kim Su-jin's decision about what the truth is - and what the show's two leads do with it - is simultaneously satisfying and uncomfortable in exactly the way the thriller's structure demanded. The resolution does not simplify either man or retroactively make either's suspicion of the other incorrect; it arrives at an understanding that acknowledges the weight of what both carried. The final address between Dong-sik and Joo-won is the episode's performance peak: Shin Ha-kyun's register in the scene is fatherly and strange and precise about the distance that remains between them even as the confrontation concludes. Beyond Evil swept the 57th Baeksang Arts Awards with Best Drama, Best Screenplay, and Best Actor, and the finale is the concentrated version of what the series earned those recognitions for.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers a resolution that feels satisfying without being clean. The show's refusal to simplify its two leads pays off in a closing hour that circles back to the town, the case, and the costs both men paid.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Dong-sik's final address to Joo-won - fatherly, strange, quietly devastating.
